prompt: You have an nmap output file scan_102.txt from scanning your Tier 0 lab VM at 192.168.56.102. Which pipeline correctly lists only the port and service name columns, for lines that are actual open-port rows?
choices: grep -E '^[0-9]+/tcp' scan_102.txt | awk '{print $1, $3}'
sort scan_102.txt | awk '{print $1}'
awk '{print $1}' scan_102.txt | grep tcp
uniq scan_102.txt | grep -v open

prompt: After merging four nmap scan files from your Tier 0 lab VMs with 'cat', which command correctly counts how many times each service name appears across all four hosts, most frequent first?
choices: grep -E '^[0-9]+/tcp' | awk '{print $3}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn
grep -E '^[0-9]+/tcp' | awk '{print $3}' | uniq -c
sort | awk '{print $3}' | grep -c tcp
awk '{print $3}' | sort -rn | uniq

prompt: Why does Kali organize its tools into metapackages like kali-tools-information-gathering, kali-tools-vulnerability, and kali-tools-exploitation, rather than grouping packages the way a default Debian install would?
choices: The categories mirror the stages of a real penetration test (recon, then vulnerability analysis, then exploitation, then post-exploitation), making the tool set match the workflow it's used for
It is required by Debian's packaging policy for all derivative distributions
It reduces the total disk space the tools occupy compared to Debian's default grouping
It is purely cosmetic branding with no effect on how the packages are installed or used

prompt: On your Tier 0 lab VM at 192.168.56.102, running 'find / -perm -4000 -type f' returns a list of files. What do those files have in common?
choices: They all have the SUID bit set, meaning they execute with their owner's privileges regardless of who runs them
They are all world-writable files that any user can modify
They are all files larger than 4000 bytes
They are all files owned by the currently logged-in user

prompt: On 192.168.56.102, 'ls -l /usr/bin/nmap' shows '-rwsr-xr-x'. What does the lowercase 's' in that permission string indicate?
choices: The SUID bit is set, so the binary runs with the privileges of its owner (root) no matter which user executes it
The file is a symbolic link to another binary
The file has been marked read-only by the system
The file's execute bit has been disabled for the owner

prompt: On your Tier 0 lab VM at 192.168.56.102, an old SUID nmap binary (version 4.53) lets a low-privileged user become root. Which feature of that old nmap version makes the escalation possible?
choices: Its interactive mode accepts '!sh' to spawn a shell, which inherits nmap's root-owned SUID privilege
It stores the root password in a plaintext config file nmap reads on startup
It automatically grants sudo access to any user who runs it once
It opens a root-owned network listener on port 4444 by default

prompt: What is the correct command to remove the SUID bit from /usr/bin/nmap on your Tier 0 lab VM at 192.168.56.102, fixing the privilege-escalation path?
choices: chmod u-s /usr/bin/nmap
chmod 777 /usr/bin/nmap
chown root:root /usr/bin/nmap
chmod +x /usr/bin/nmap

prompt: In the lab_sweep.sh script, 'for ip in "${LAB_IPS[@]}"; do ... done' loops over the array of lab VM addresses. What does the '[@]' expansion do?
choices: It expands the array into each of its individual elements, so the loop body runs once per IP address
It sorts the array elements alphabetically before the loop begins
It converts the array into a single space-free string
It limits the loop to only the first element of the array
